title: Problem Solving & Coding Patterns in Go — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Coding pattern questions are the most time-pressured part of a Go fresher interview. You have 20-30 minutes to write a working solution, and interviewers are watching how you use the language — not just whether you get the right answer. Knowing the idiomatic Go approach for FizzBuzz, palindrome checking, two-sum, and string reversal means you spend your time thinking about the algorithm, not fighting Go syntax.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three Go idioms that appear in almost every coding problem:

- **Use a map for O(1) lookup.** Two-sum, frequency counting, anagram detection, duplicate finding — all solved with `make(map[T]int)` or `make(map[T]bool)`. The `v, ok := m[key]` existence check is essential.
- **Use `[]rune` for Unicode-safe string mutation.** `s[i]` gives bytes; `[]rune(s)[i]` gives characters. For palindrome, reverse, and anagram problems involving non-ASCII text, always convert to `[]rune` first.
- **Use `strings.Fields` for word splitting.** It handles multiple spaces, tabs, and leading/trailing whitespace — unlike `strings.Split(s, " ")` which produces empty strings for consecutive spaces. For word count problems, `strings.Fields` is almost always the right tool.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **FizzBuzz in Go** — `for i := 1; i <= 100; i++` with `switch { case i%15==0: ... case i%3==0: ... case i%5==0: ... default: fmt.Println(i) }` — switch without a condition is the clean Go idiom
- **Fibonacci iterative** — `a, b := 0, 1; for i := 0; i < n; i++ { a, b = b, a+b }` — idiomatic multiple assignment in Go; iterative is preferred over recursive to avoid stack growth
- **Palindrome check** — convert to `[]rune` for Unicode safety; `left, right := 0, len(r)-1; for left < right { if r[left] != r[right] { return false }; left++; right-- }`
- **Anagram check** — `make(map[rune]int)` frequency count of first string; decrement for second; check all values are zero
- **Two-sum** — `seen := make(map[int]int)` mapping value to index; `if j, ok := seen[target-nums[i]]; ok { return []int{j, i} }; seen[nums[i]] = i`
- **Reverse string** — `r := []rune(s); for i, j := 0, len(r)-1; i < j; i, j = i+1, j-1 { r[i], r[j] = r[j], r[i] }; return string(r)`
- **Count words** — `words := strings.Fields(s); freq := make(map[string]int); for _, w := range words { freq[strings.ToLower(w)]++ }`

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **FizzBuzz with switch vs if-else** — using a switch without a condition expression (`switch { case ... }`) is more idiomatic Go than a chain of `if/else if`. Interviewers notice this as a signal you know Go idioms.
- **Recursive Fibonacci and stack depth** — for large `n`, recursion hits Go's goroutine stack limit (which grows dynamically but is still finite). Interviewers ask: 'what is the time complexity?' — O(2^n) recursive vs O(n) iterative. Always mention you prefer iterative.
- **Palindrome on `"café"` with byte indexing** — `s[0] == s[len(s)-1]` on a multi-byte string compares bytes, not characters. This gives wrong answers for non-ASCII input. The correct approach uses `[]rune`.
- **Word count with `strings.Split(s, " ")`** — `"hello  world"` (double space) produces an empty string element. `strings.Fields` handles all whitespace and produces no empty strings. Using Fields shows you know the standard library.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"For coding problems in Go, my go-to tools are: a `make(map[T]int)` for frequency counting or O(1) lookup, `[]rune` conversion before any string indexing or mutation to handle Unicode correctly, `strings.Fields` for splitting on whitespace, and multiple assignment for swaps — `a, b = b, a` without a temp variable. For FizzBuzz I use a `switch { case i%15==0: ... }` without a condition expression, which is the idiomatic Go way to write conditional logic that does not fit a single expression."*
